lesson.title: The Second Burden: Stigma in Mental Health
lesson.summary: Stigma, negative stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination directed at people with psychological disorders, is a serious barrier to treatment and recovery in its own right, separate from the symptoms of the disorder itself.
lesson.body:
The same basic building blocks used to describe prejudice and discrimination generally apply directly to mental illness. A stereotype is a belief, prejudice is a negative attitude or feeling, and discrimination is the behavioral expression of that attitude. A person living with a diagnosed psychological disorder can face stereotyping, being assumed to be dangerous, unpredictable, or weak, none of which is accurate as a general characterization of people with psychological disorders, alongside negative attitudes and concrete discrimination in employment, housing, relationships, or access to health care.

Researchers distinguish public stigma, the attitudes held by society at large, from self-stigma or internalized stigma, a pattern studied extensively by researchers including Patrick Corrigan, in which a person absorbs those negative societal messages and applies them to themselves. Internalized stigma can lower self-esteem and self-efficacy, and importantly, it can itself become a barrier that keeps someone from seeking treatment in the first place, worsening the very difficulties stigma claims to be reacting to. There is also structural stigma to consider: policies and institutional practices, such as historically limited insurance coverage for mental health treatment, that disadvantage people with psychological disorders even without any single individual holding a consciously prejudiced attitude.

This connects back to the difficulty of defining a psychological disorder discussed earlier. The deviance criterion, judging behavior as disordered partly because it departs from cultural norms, is precisely the kind of judgment that can shade into stigma when applied carelessly or extended beyond what is clinically warranted. Behavior being unusual is not the same as it being dangerous or something to be feared, and stigma often flattens that distinction in ways that cause real harm.

Research broadly points to a few consistent factors in reducing stigma: accurate education about psychological disorders, and direct contact with people who have lived experience of a psychological disorder, both tend to reduce stigmatizing attitudes more reliably than providing information alone. Changing public language and media portrayal is also frequently discussed as a lever worth pursuing, though its effects are harder to measure directly than those of controlled educational or contact-based interventions, so it is fair to treat that particular claim as reasonable but less firmly established.
